title: What is @SecondaryTable, how does it let one entity span multiple tables, and when should you use it?
shortTitle: @SecondaryTable — mapping a single entity across multiple tables

s1_definition.profdef: `@SecondaryTable` lets a SINGLE JPA entity map its fields across TWO OR MORE physical tables that share the same primary key. The primary `@Table` holds the main columns; each `@SecondaryTable(name = ..., pkJoinColumns = @PrimaryKeyJoinColumn(...))` declares an additional table joined on the primary key, and you route individual fields to it with `@Column(table = "secondary_table_name")`. Hibernate transparently joins the tables on read and splits the writes across them on save, so to the application it looks like one entity. You use it when a logical record is physically split across tables — often for legacy schemas, for separating hot frequently-accessed columns from cold rarely-accessed ones, or for isolating large/sensitive columns (like KYC documents) into their own table while still modelling them as one entity.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer's full record at National Bank of India is one logical thing, but the data lives in two filing cabinets: the everyday cabinet holds name and balance, while a separate secure cabinet holds the KYC documents and address proof. `@SecondaryTable` is the clerk who knows both cabinets belong to the same customer number, fetches from both when you ask for the customer, and files into both when you update — so you deal with one customer, not two cabinets.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@SecondaryTable` maps one entity across multiple tables sharing the primary key; route fields with `@Column(table = "...")`, and Hibernate joins on read and splits on write automatically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@SecondaryTable` lets a SINGLE JPA entity map its fields across TWO OR MORE physical tables that share the same primary key. The primary `@Table` holds the main columns; each `@SecondaryTable(name = ..., pkJoinColumns = @PrimaryKeyJoinColumn(...))` declares an additional table joined on the primary key, and you route individual fields to it with `@Column(table = "secondary_table_name")`. Hibernate transparently joins the tables on read and splits the writes across them on save, so to the application it looks like one entity. You use it when a logical record is physically split across tables — often for legacy schemas, for separating hot frequently-accessed columns from cold rarely-accessed ones, or for isolating large/sensitive columns (like KYC documents) into their own table while still modelling them as one entity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A customer's full record at National Bank of India is one logical thing, but the data lives in two filing cabinets: the everyday cabinet holds name and balance, while a separate secure cabinet holds the KYC documents and address proof. `@SecondaryTable` is the clerk who knows both cabinets belong to the same customer number, fetches from both when you ask for the customer, and files into both when you update — so you deal with one customer, not two cabinets.

**One line to remember:** `@SecondaryTable` maps one entity across multiple tables sharing the primary key; route fields with `@Column(table = "...")`, and Hibernate joins on read and splits on write automatically.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the exact situation at National Bank of India that made `@SecondaryTable` the right fit.

Problem 1 — a legacy split we could not easily merge. Historically, core account data lived in an `accounts` table while KYC data (PAN, address proof, document blobs) lived in a separate `account_kyc` table keyed by the same account id. Two teams owned the two tables, and merging them physically was out of scope. But in the new service we wanted to treat an account as one clean entity, not juggle two. This is exactly what `@SecondaryTable` provides: one entity transparently spanning both tables on the shared primary key.

Problem 2 — KYC columns were bloating the common queries. The account listing and balance screens are called constantly and only need name and balance, yet the old two-entity model sometimes dragged the heavy KYC document text along. This is exactly where routing KYC columns to a secondary table helps: the common columns stay in the narrow primary table.

Problem 3 — sensitive data needed tighter isolation. PAN and document blobs are sensitive and the security team wanted them in a table with stricter grants. This is exactly where a secondary table helps: the sensitive columns live in `account_kyc` which can carry its own access controls, while the entity still models everything as one `Account`.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity with `@Table(name = "accounts")` and `@SecondaryTable(name = "account_kyc", pkJoinColumns = @PrimaryKeyJoinColumn(name = "account_id"))`. The common fields (`holderName`, `balance`) map to the primary table; the KYC fields (`pan`, `aadhaarDoc`) are routed with `@Column(table = "account_kyc")`. The `AccountService`, annotated `@Transactional`, opens an account with both common and KYC data, and reads it back, showing one entity assembled from both tables. The demo shows Hibernate issuing an INSERT into each table on save and a JOIN on read. A test verifies the KYC fields carry the `table` attribute pointing at the secondary table.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package

# Run
java -jar target/account-kyc-service-1.0.0.jar

# Open an account — writes split across BOTH tables
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8366/api/v1/kyc-accounts?accountId=SAV3001&holderName=Amit%20Patel&balance=500000&pan=KLMNO9012P&aadhaarDoc=scan-data"
# SQL: INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, holder_name, balance) VALUES (...)
#      INSERT INTO account_kyc (account_id, pan, aadhaar_doc) VALUES (...)

# View — JOIN assembles one entity from both tables
curl http://localhost:8366/api/v1/kyc-accounts/SAV2001
# SQL: SELECT ... FROM accounts a JOIN account_kyc k ON a.account_id = k.account_id WHERE a.account_id = 'SAV2001'
# → {"accountId":"SAV2001","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":1000000.00,"pan":"ABCDE1234F","hasAadhaarDoc":true}

# Run tests
mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is opening Amit's account with common data and KYC data, then viewing Rajesh's account.

Step 1: `open(...)` runs in a `@Transactional` method and constructs one `Account` carrying both the common fields (holder name, balance) and the KYC fields (PAN, Aadhaar document).

Step 2: `accountRepo.save(account)` triggers Hibernate to split the write across two tables. It issues `INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, holder_name, balance) VALUES ('SAV3001', 'Amit Patel', 500000)` for the primary-table fields, and `INSERT INTO account_kyc (account_id, pan, aadhaar_doc) VALUES ('SAV3001', 'KLMNO9012P', 'scan-data')` for the fields routed with `@Column(table = "account_kyc")`. Both rows share the same primary key `SAV3001`.

Step 3: From the application's point of view this was a single `save` of a single entity; the two-table physical layout is invisible to the caller.

Step 4: The view flow loads Rajesh's account. Hibernate generates a JOIN: `SELECT a.account_id, a.holder_name, a.balance, k.pan, k.aadhaar_doc FROM accounts a JOIN account_kyc k ON a.account_id = k.account_id WHERE a.account_id = 'SAV2001'`. It assembles one `Account` object whose common fields come from the `accounts` table and whose KYC fields come from the `account_kyc` table.

Step 5: The service maps to an `AccountKycView` record. The PAN, which physically lives in the secondary table, appears as an ordinary field on the one logical account, demonstrating the transparency `@SecondaryTable` provides. The view does not expose the raw document; it reports only whether a document exists, keeping sensitive data out of the response.

```
  @Column (no table)              → primary table  (accounts)

  INSERT INTO accounts    (account_id, holder_name, balance)
  INSERT INTO account_kyc (account_id, pan, aadhaar_doc)

  ── WHEN TO USE ──
  legacy split schema | hot/cold column separation | sensitive-data isolation
```

```
  Rule: @SecondaryTable for legacy/vertical split; lazy @OneToOne if cold data is rare.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
SecondaryTable lets a single JPA entity map its fields across two or more physical tables that share the same primary key. I declare the main table with the Table annotation and each extra table with a SecondaryTable annotation, telling it the join column with a PrimaryKeyJoinColumn so the secondary table's primary key is also a foreign key back to the primary. Then I route individual fields to the secondary table with the table attribute on the Column annotation, while fields without that attribute default to the primary table. On a read Hibernate generates a join on the shared key and assembles one entity, and on a save it splits the inserts or updates across both tables, so the whole two-table layout is invisible to the application code.

I reach for this in three situations. The first is a legacy schema where a record was historically split across two tables and I want to model it as one clean entity rather than juggling two entities with a one-to-one relationship. The second is separating hot frequently-read columns from cold rarely-read bulky columns, keeping the common queries fast. The third is isolating sensitive data into its own table that can carry stricter access controls while still presenting a single entity to the code. In our account service at National Bank of India, the accounts table holds name and balance, and a secondary account_kyc table holds the PAN and document blobs, yet the code deals with one Account entity.

The senior cautions I always raise are that the secondary table is joined eagerly by default, so if the secondary columns are genuinely cold it may be cleaner to model them as a lazy one-to-one association that loads only when touched; that I must ensure a secondary row exists or the columns are nullable to avoid join mismatches producing nulls; and crucially that SecondaryTable is a mapping convenience, not a sharding or scaling mechanism, because both tables live in the same database and are joined within the same transaction. For real scaling I would look at partitioning or splitting services, not secondary tables.
